Project Atlas – Evidence Gallery v0.1

Purpose

The Evidence Gallery is a curated collection of real-world compositions that are analyzed using Atlas principles. It complements scientific literature by showing how those principles appear in practice.

The gallery does not prove a principle. Instead, it provides observable examples that can be explained by the current Atlas model.

Gallery Entry Format

Each entry should contain:

  • Gallery ID
  • Source
  • Domain
  • Screenshot (when licensing permits)
  • Atlas principles involved
  • Observed strengths
  • Observed weaknesses
  • Competing organizations
  • Confidence
  • Supporting literature
  • Open questions

Evidence Gallery 0001

GOV.UK Forms

Domain: Government web forms

Atlas Principles

  • ATLAS-0001 Relative Separation
  • Candidate: Hierarchical Spacing Differentiation

Observations

Positive evidence:

  • Strong separation between sections.
  • Consistent internal spacing.
  • Large section headings.
  • Minimal competing organizations.
  • Reinforcing cues (spacing + headings).

Atlas Interpretation

The layout uses multiple compatible grouping cues instead of relying on whitespace alone.

Confidence: High

Research to connect:

  • Gestalt proximity
  • Common region
  • Visual hierarchy
  • Form usability

Evidence Gallery 0002

Apple Settings

Domain: Mobile OS

Atlas Principles

  • Relative Separation
  • Hierarchical grouping
  • Cue reinforcement

Observations

Positive evidence:

  • Clear section boundaries.
  • Repeating spacing rhythm.
  • Typography reinforces grouping.
  • Controls naturally cluster.

Atlas predicts these reduce ambiguity during rapid scanning.

Confidence: Moderate–High

Evidence Gallery 0003

Uniform-Spacing Forms (Negative Pattern)

Domain: Generic web applications

Pattern

Many criticized forms use nearly identical spacing for:

  • labels
  • fields
  • sections
  • actions

Atlas Diagnosis

The layout contains multiple semantic levels but communicates nearly one spacing level.

Result:

  • Flattened hierarchy.
  • Increased competing organizations.
  • Users depend on headings rather than geometry.

Confidence: Moderate

Emerging Research Direction

One unexpected observation emerged from comparing modern design systems.

Most systems define spacing tokens such as:

  • 4
  • 8
  • 12
  • 16
  • 24
  • 32
  • 48

They describe what values to use but rarely explain why those values produce reliable perceptual organization.

Atlas should investigate the underlying mechanisms rather than treating the tokens themselves as universal rules.

New Candidate Research Questions

  1. Why do independent design systems converge on similar spacing scales?
  2. Are spacing scales driven by biology, convention, implementation, or all three?
  3. Which spacing relationships remain stable across web, mobile, print, dashboards, and architecture?
  4. Can Atlas derive spacing recommendations from perceptual mechanisms rather than fixed design tokens?

Next Collection Priorities

  1. GOV.UK Design System
  2. Apple Human Interface Guidelines
  3. Material Design
  4. IBM Carbon Design System
  5. Microsoft Fluent
  6. NASA cockpit/HMI guidance
  7. Medical interfaces
  8. Financial trading platforms
  9. Information graphics
  10. Museum and wayfinding systems

Atlas Insight

The first comparisons suggest that mature design systems independently converge on many of the same structural patterns:

  • stronger spacing between groups than within groups;
  • multiple reinforcing grouping cues;
  • nested hierarchy;
  • consistent spacing scales.

Atlas's role is to explain why these convergent patterns work, determine their limits, and identify the perceptual mechanisms behind them rather than simply documenting best practices.

Built from Markdown with a reusable Astro and Pagefind workflow.
